medium.q: Explain why the steel car is always attracted to the magnet and never repelled.
medium.model_answer: The magnet induces magnetism in the steel. The end nearest the magnet becomes the opposite pole, so it is always attracted.

medium.q: Why is soft iron, not steel, used for the core of an electromagnet?
medium.model_answer: Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily (a temporary magnet), so the electromagnet can be switched off.

medium.q: Name three ways to make an electromagnet stronger.
medium.model_answer: More turns on the coil, a bigger current, and a soft iron core.

medium.q: How can you prove an object is a magnet and not just a piece of iron?
medium.model_answer: Show that it repels a known magnet. Repulsion only happens between two magnets; iron is only ever attracted.

medium.q: Our car weighs 0.5 N and the track has μ = 0.2. Work out the friction force.
Explain why a charged ruler can pick up small pieces of neutral paper.
medium.model_answer: It induces opposite charge on the near side of the paper. That side is closer, so the attraction is bigger than the repulsion.

medium.q: Describe the magnetic field around a straight wire carrying a current.
medium.model_answer: Circles centred on the wire. Reversing the current reverses the field direction.

medium.q: Name two magnetic metals and two non-magnetic metals.
medium.model_answer: Magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt. Non-magnetic: e.g. copper, aluminium, brass, gold.

medium.q: A polythene rod rubbed with a cloth becomes negative. What happened to the cloth, and why?
medium.model_answer: Electrons moved from the cloth to the rod, so the cloth is left positively charged.

medium.q: Why must you hold the magnet closer to pull the car over a sandpaper patch?
medium.model_answer: Sandpaper gives more friction (0.3 N instead of 0.1 N). The pull is stronger closer, so it can beat the friction.

hard.q: State Fleming's left-hand rule. What does each finger show?
hard.model_answer: First finger = field, second finger = current, thumb = force (motion). Used for the motor effect.

hard.q: How do you work out which end of a solenoid is the north pole?
hard.model_answer: Right-hand grip rule: curl your fingers the way the current flows; your thumb points to the north pole.

hard.q: Explain how a steel sheet screens the car from the magnet.
hard.model_answer: Field lines are drawn into the steel (an easy path), so very few pass to the space behind it. The field there is weak.

hard.q: A magnet is pushed into a coil connected to a meter. Give two ways to increase the induced e.m.f.
hard.model_answer: Any two: move the magnet faster, use a stronger magnet, use more turns on the coil.

hard.q: Why does the car suddenly jump towards the magnet once it gets close?
hard.model_answer: Magnetic force rises very quickly as distance gets smaller, so up close the pull grows much bigger than friction.

hard.q: Describe the magnetic field inside and outside a long solenoid.
hard.model_answer: Inside: strong and uniform, straight parallel lines. Outside: the same shape as a bar magnet's field.

hard.q: Why can't you charge a metal rod by rubbing it while holding it in your hand?
hard.model_answer: Metal is a conductor, so the charge flows through you to earth.

hard.q: A 50 g car has 0.3 N of friction and a 0.45 N magnetic pull. Find its acceleration.
hard.model_answer: Resultant force = 0.45 − 0.3 = 0.15 N. a = F ÷ m = 0.15 ÷ 0.05 = 3 m/s².

hard.q: Find the force on a 0.1 m wire carrying 2 A at right angles to a 0.5 T field.
Two charged balloons are moved twice as far apart. What happens to the force between them?
hard.model_answer: It becomes ¼ as big, because electric force ∝ 1/r² (inverse square law).
